```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", dev = "png",
                      fig.retina = 2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5,
                      fig.align = "center")
library(mlvtoolbox)
```

A *junction* is a place where two or more distinct contours meet or cross: the
corner where a wall meets the floor, the T where one object occludes another,
the X where two wires cross. Junction type and junction angle are used as
predictors of scene categorization
([Walther et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomp.2023.1140723)), and
`mlvtoolbox` reports them for every drawing. This vignette explains how
`detect_junctions()` finds junctions, what an *arm* is, how the type and
angles follow from the arms, and where the default rule differs from the
published MLV toolbox. The drawings are small enough that every answer can be
derived by hand before reading the output.

Angles follow the drawing convention used throughout the package: degrees
counterclockwise from the rightward x axis as seen on screen, with image y
pointing down. An arm pointing right has orientation 0, up 90, left 180 and
down 270.

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
seg <- function(...) matrix(c(...), ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE)
# The defaults of detect_junctions(), read rather than retyped.
defaults <- formals(detect_junctions)
eps <- defaults$absolute_epsilon; rel_eps <- defaults$relative_epsilon
nbhd <- defaults$endpoint_radius; merge_r <- defaults$merge_radius
polyline <- function(x, y) {
  n <- length(x)
  cbind(x1 = x[-n], y1 = y[-n], x2 = x[-1], y2 = y[-1])
}
# Point at distance r from (cx, cy) in direction a (degrees, y down).
ray <- function(a, r = 14, cx = 20, cy = 20) c(cx + r * cospi(a / 180), cy - r * sinpi(a / 180))
okabe <- c(orange = "#E69F00", sky = "#56B4E9", green = "#009E73",
           blue = "#0072B2", vermilion = "#D55E00", purple = "#CC79A7")
disc <- function(x, y, r, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("grey50", 0.15),
                 border = "grey55", ...) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 97)
  for (k in seq_along(x)) polygon(x[k] + r * cos(t), y[k] + r * sin(t),
                                  col = col, border = border, lwd = 0.6, ...)
}
# The phone-width copy of each figure is a replay of the desktop drawing, so
# anything measured from the device (text widths, inches, the device width)
# is drawn through recordGraphics(), which re-evaluates it on replay.
replay <- function(f, ...) {
  args <- list(...)
  recordGraphics(do.call(f, args), list(f = f, args = args), globalenv())
}
# A panel title, shortened when the device is narrow.
fit_title <- function(wide, narrow = wide) replay(function(wide, narrow)
  title(main = if (par("din")[1] < 5) narrow else wide, cex.main = 1, font.main = 1),
  wide = wide, narrow = narrow)
# A pixel-scale view around a point: no frame, faint pixel boundaries.
loupe <- function(d, centre, half, main = "", ..., short = main, grid = TRUE, lwd = 2) {
  plot(d, axes = FALSE, frame = FALSE, pixel_grid = grid, lwd = lwd,
       xlim = centre[1] + c(-half, half), ylim = centre[2] + c(half, -half), ...)
  fit_title(main, short)
}
# Dimension line from p to q, offset `off` px to one side, with end ticks;
# the label sits beyond the line on the same side.
dimension <- function(...) replay(dimension_now, ...)
dimension_now <- function(p, q, label, off = 0.4, col = "grey15", cex = 0.75, gap = 0.25) {
  u <- (q - p) / sqrt(sum((q - p)^2)); n <- c(-u[2], u[1]) * sign(off)
  a <- p + abs(off) * n; b <- q + abs(off) * n; t <- 0.13 * n
  segments(a[1], a[2], b[1], b[2], col = col, lwd = 0.9)
  segments(c(a[1], b[1]) - t[1], c(a[2], b[2]) - t[2],
           c(a[1], b[1]) + t[1], c(a[2], b[2]) + t[2], col = col, lwd = 0.9)
  m <- (a + b) / 2 + gap * n
  # y points down, so a label below the line hangs from its top edge.
  adj <- c(if (abs(n[1]) < 0.3) 0.5 else if (n[1] > 0) 0 else 1,
           if (abs(n[2]) < 0.3) 0.5 else if (n[2] > 0) 1 else 0)
  if (nzchar(label)) {
    # A white box behind the label; "up" on screen is +up in user y.
    w <- strwidth(label, cex = cex); h <- abs(strheight(label, cex = cex))
    up <- sign(diff(par("usr")[3:4])); bottom <- m[2] - adj[2] * h * up
    rect(m[1] - adj[1] * w - 0.1 * h, bottom - 0.15 * h * up,
         m[1] + (1 - adj[1]) * w + 0.1 * h, bottom + 1.15 * h * up, col = "white", border = NA)
  }
  text(m[1], m[2], label, adj = adj, cex = cex, col = col)
}
# Directions in which contours leave a meeting point that is not a junction,
# drawn like arms but in grey.
exits <- function(...) replay(exits_now, ...)
exits_now <- function(x, y, angles, len, col = "grey40") {
  upi <- diff(par("usr")[1:2]) / par("pin")[1]; h <- 0.075 * upi; w <- 0.045 * upi
  for (k in seq_along(angles)) {
    r <- angles[k] * pi / 180; ex <- x[k] + len * cos(r); ey <- y[k] - len * sin(r)
    segments(x[k], y[k], ex - 0.6 * h * cos(r), ey + 0.6 * h * sin(r), lwd = 5, lend = 1,
             col = grDevices::adjustcolor(col, 0.35))
    bx <- ex - h * cos(r); by <- ey + h * sin(r)
    polygon(c(ex, bx - w * sin(r), bx + w * sin(r)), c(ey, by - w * cos(r), by + w * cos(r)),
            col = col, border = NA)
  }
}
# The whole drawing, scaled into box = c(x0, y0, x1, y1) of the current panel,
# with the panel's own window outlined.
inset <- function(d, box, window) {
  xy <- do.call(rbind, d$contours)
  xr <- range(xy[, c(1, 3)], window[c(1, 3)]); yr <- range(xy[, c(2, 4)], window[c(2, 4)])
  s <- min((box[3] - box[1]) / diff(xr), (box[4] - box[2]) / diff(yr))
  fx <- function(v) box[1] + (v - xr[1]) * s; fy <- function(v) box[2] + (v - yr[1]) * s
  rect(box[1] - 0.25, box[2] - 0.25, fx(xr[2]) + 0.25, fy(yr[2]) + 0.25,
       col = "white", border = "grey70", lwd = 0.6)
  segments(fx(xy[, 1]), fy(xy[, 2]), fx(xy[, 3]), fy(xy[, 4]), lwd = 1)
  rect(fx(window[1]), fy(window[2]), fx(window[3]), fy(window[4]),
       border = "grey45", lty = 3, lwd = 0.7)
}
```

## From crossings to junctions

`detect_junctions()` works in four steps.

1. **Intersections.** It finds every point where a segment of one contour
   meets or crosses a segment of a different contour. Before testing, each
   end of every segment may be extended by a small *gap allowance*, so a
   stroke that stops just short of another still meets it. Crossings within one
   contour and collinear overlaps are not junctions.
2. **Merging.** Intersections within `merge_radius` (default 2 pixels) of
   each other are merged into one junction, transitively, so a chain of close crossings
   becomes a single junction at their mean position.
3. **Arms.** The *junction neighbourhood* is the union of open discs of radius
   `endpoint_radius` (default 2 pixels) around the merged intersections. Each
   incident contour contributes one *arm* for each direction in which it
   leaves the neighbourhood. An arm's orientation is the direction of the
   segment through which the contour leaves, pointing away from the junction.
4. **Classification.** A junction needs at least three arms. Sorting the arm
   orientations gives the *angles*, the gaps between consecutive arms, which
   sum to 360 degrees. Three arms make a Y when the largest gap is under 160
   degrees, a T when it is between 160 and 200, and an Arrow when it exceeds
   200; four arms make an X and five or more a Star.

Each row of the result is one junction, with its position, type, smallest and
largest gap (`min_angle`, `max_angle`), and three list columns: `arms` (sorted
arm orientations), `angles` (gaps; `angles[k]` runs from `arms[k]` to the next
arm counterclockwise) and `members` (the incident contour segments).

```{r t-junction}
t_shape <- mlv_drawing(list(bar = seg(6, 20, 34, 20), stem = seg(20, 20, 20, 34)),
                       width = 40, height = 40)
j <- detect_junctions(t_shape)
j[, c("x", "y", "type", "min_angle", "max_angle")]
j$arms[[1]]
j$angles[[1]]
```

The bar leaves the neighbourhood to the right (0 degrees) and to the left
(180); the stem leaves downward (270). Sorted, the arms are 0, 180 and 270,
so the gaps are 180, 90 and 90 degrees. The largest gap is 180, so this is a
T.

## A gallery of junction types

```{r gallery-build}
gallery <- list(
  L = list(seg(20, 20, 34, 20), seg(20, 20, 20, 6)),
  T = list(seg(6, 20, 34, 20), seg(20, 20, 20, 34)),
  X = list(seg(6, 20, 34, 20), seg(20, 6, 20, 34)),
  Y = list(rbind(c(ray(90), 20, 20), c(20, 20, ray(210))), seg(20, 20, ray(330))),
  Arrow = list(rbind(c(ray(210), 20, 20), c(20, 20, ray(330))), seg(20, 20, ray(270))),
  Star = list(seg(ray(0), ray(180)), seg(ray(60), ray(240)), seg(ray(120), ray(300))))
gallery <- lapply(gallery, mlv_drawing, width = 40, height = 40)
found <- lapply(gallery, detect_junctions)
data.frame(drawing = names(found),
           junctions = vapply(found, nrow, 1L),
           type = vapply(found, function(j) if (nrow(j)) j$type else "none", ""),
           arms = vapply(found, function(j) if (nrow(j)) length(j$arms[[1]]) else 0L, 1L),
           max_angle = vapply(found, function(j) if (nrow(j)) round(j$max_angle, 1) else NA, 1))
```

```{r gallery-check, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(unname(vapply(found, function(j) if (nrow(j)) j$type else "none", "")),
                    c("none", "T", "X", "Y", "Arrow", "Star")))
# A three-arm junction whose largest gap is L: one arm straight down, two at
# 270 +/- (360 - L) / 2. Its type, as detect_junctions() reports it.
three_arms <- function(L, r = 12) {
  h <- (360 - L) / 2
  mlv_drawing(list(rbind(c(ray(270 - h, r), 20, 20), c(20, 20, ray(270 + h, r))),
                   seg(20, 20, ray(270, r))), 40, 40)
}
type_of <- function(L) detect_junctions(three_arms(L))$type
# The Y/T and T/Arrow limits, found by bisection on the package's own answer.
limit <- function(lo, hi) {
  below <- type_of(lo)
  for (i in 1:40) { mid <- (lo + hi) / 2; if (type_of(mid) == below) lo <- mid else hi <- mid }
  (lo + hi) / 2
}
limits <- c(YT = limit(130, 175), TA = limit(185, 230))
stopifnot(abs(limits - c(160, 200)) < 1e-6)
morph_gaps <- c(125, 130, 150, 170, 180, 190, 210, 230, 240)
```

```{r fig-gallery, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = sprintf("Six drawings of two or three contours, with each junction's arms (orange) and the gaps between them. Among three arms the largest gap sets the type: %g° makes a T and %g° an Arrow (shaded), while the Y's largest gap, %g°, is under the %g° limit. The L leaves its corner only twice (grey arrows), so it is not a junction.", round(found$T$max_angle), round(found$Arrow$max_angle), round(found$Y$max_angle), round(limits[["YT"]]))}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.8, 0.2))
par(cex = 0.85)
for (name in names(gallery)) {
  j <- found[[name]]
  title <- if (nrow(j)) sprintf("%s, %d arms", j$type, length(j$arms[[1]])) else
    "L, 2 arms: no junction"
  xy <- do.call(rbind, gallery[[name]]$contours)
  mid <- c(mean(range(xy[, c(1, 3)])), mean(range(xy[, c(2, 4)])))
  plot(gallery[[name]], property = "junctions", arms = TRUE, gaps = TRUE,
       arm_length = 9, axes = FALSE, frame = FALSE, lwd = 2,
       xlim = mid[1] + c(-15.5, 15.5), ylim = mid[2] + c(15.5, -15.5))
  fit_title(title, if (nrow(j)) title else "L: no junction")
  if (!nrow(j)) exits(c(20, 20), c(20, 20), c(0, 90), 9)
}
par(op)
```

The L is a meeting of two contours, but it has only two arms, so it is not
reported; neither is a corner within a single contour. The Y, T and Arrow all
have three arms and differ only in how those arms are spread: equal 120 degree
gaps (Y), a straight bar with a stem (T, largest gap 180), and three arms
within a half-plane (Arrow, largest gap 240). Four arms always make an X and
the six arms of three crossing lines a Star, whatever their angles.

The three-arm types are bands of one continuum, not three shapes. Opening the
two upper arms of a junction step by step sweeps its largest gap from
`r min(morph_gaps)`° to `r max(morph_gaps)`°; the type changes where the largest gap crosses
`r round(limits[["YT"]])`° (Y to T) and passes
`r round(limits[["TA"]])`° (T to Arrow). Both limits above were found by
bisection on `detect_junctions()` itself.

```{r fig-morph, fig.height = 2.5, fig.cap = sprintf("Nine three-arm junctions whose largest gap grows from %g° to %g°, each typed by detect_junctions(), and their positions on a line of largest gap. A T is not one shape but a %g° band of shapes, between the %g° and %g° limits; the shaded sector in each junction is its largest gap.", min(morph_gaps), max(morph_gaps), round(diff(limits)), round(limits[["YT"]]), round(limits[["TA"]]))}
morph_types <- vapply(morph_gaps, type_of, "")
type_cols <- c(Y = "grey35", T = "black", Arrow = "grey35")
layout(rbind(seq_along(morph_gaps), length(morph_gaps) + 1), heights = c(1, lcm(1.9)))
op <- par(mar = c(0, 0.1, 1.4, 0.1), cex = 0.85)
for (k in seq_along(morph_gaps)) {
  plot(three_arms(morph_gaps[k]), property = "junctions", arms = TRUE, gaps = "max",
       arm_length = 8, axes = FALSE, frame = FALSE, lwd = 2,
       xlim = c(7, 33), ylim = c(33, 7))
  fit_title(morph_types[k])
}
# The number line of largest gap, with the type limits and each junction.
par(mar = c(1.6, 0.1, 0.2, 0.1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, length(morph_gaps) + 0.5), ylim = c(0, 1), axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
scale_x <- function(L) 1 + (L - 120) / (245 - 120) * (length(morph_gaps) - 1)
rect(scale_x(limits[["YT"]]), 0.25, scale_x(limits[["TA"]]), 0.45, col = "grey88", border = NA)
segments(scale_x(120), 0.35, scale_x(245), 0.35, col = "grey40")
segments(scale_x(limits), 0.18, scale_x(limits), 0.52, lwd = 1.5)
text(scale_x(limits), 0.6, paste0(round(limits), "°"), adj = c(0.5, 0), cex = 0.8)
text(scale_x(c(140, mean(limits), 222)), 0.06, c("Y", "T", "Arrow"), cex = 0.8,
     col = "grey30", adj = c(0.5, 0))
# A leader from each junction (above) to its largest gap on the line.
segments(seq_along(morph_gaps), 1, scale_x(morph_gaps), 0.35, col = "grey70", lwd = 0.7)
points(scale_x(morph_gaps), rep(0.35, length(morph_gaps)), pch = 19, cex = 0.6)
mtext("largest gap (°)", side = 1, line = 0.4, cex = 0.7, col = "grey30")
par(op)
layout(1)
```

## The gap allowance

Hand-drawn and traced contours rarely meet exactly. A stem that stops half a
pixel short of a bar is still a T to a viewer, so before intersecting, each
end of every segment may be extended by up to `absolute_epsilon` pixels
(default 1) and by at most `relative_epsilon` of the segment's own length
(default 0.3); the stricter of the two limits applies.

```{r gap}
gaps <- mlv_drawing(list(bar = seg(4, 10, 36, 10),
                         near = seg(12, 10.5, 12, 22),
                         far = seg(28, 11.5, 28, 22)),
                    width = 40, height = 24)
detect_junctions(gaps)[, c("x", "y", "type")]
```

```{r gap-check, include = FALSE}
gj <- detect_junctions(gaps)
stopifnot(nrow(gj) == 1L, gj$x == 12)
```

The stem at x = 12 stops 0.5 pixels below the bar, inside the 1 pixel
allowance, and forms a T at (12, 10). The stem at x = 28 stops 1.5 pixels
short and forms no junction. The relative limit matters for short segments:
a segment 2 pixels long can be extended by at most 0.6 pixels.

The allowance applies to both ends of every segment, not only to the free
ends of a contour. A V whose vertex stops 0.5 pixels below the bar meets it
through the extension of both of its segments and leaves the neighbourhood
twice, so it forms an X:

```{r interior-vertex}
v_shape <- mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 10, 35, 10),
                            polyline(c(12, 20, 28), c(25, 10.5, 25))), 40, 30)
detect_junctions(v_shape)[, c("x", "y", "type")]
```

```{r interior-check, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(detect_junctions(v_shape)$type == "X")
```

```{r fig-gap, fig.height = 2.9, fig.cap = sprintf("The gap allowance at pixel scale; grid lines are pixel boundaries. A stem's end may extend along the stem by up to %g px (blue, to the dashed outline). Left: a stem %g px short reaches the bar and forms a T (dot). Right: a stem %g px short still stops %g px short, so there is no junction.", eps, near_gap, far_gap, far_gap - eps)}
near_gap <- 10.5 - 10; far_gap <- 11.5 - 10
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.8, 0.2))
for (x0 in c(12, 28)) {
  short <- if (x0 == 12) near_gap else far_gap
  loupe(gaps, c(x0, 11.2), 2.6, property = "junctions", reach = "euclidean",
        main = sprintf("%g px short: %s", short, if (x0 == 12) "T" else "no junction"),
        short = sprintf("%g px short: %s", short, if (x0 == 12) "T" else "none"))
  dimension(c(x0, 10 + short), c(x0, 10), sprintf("%g px", short), off = -1.2)
  if (x0 == 28) {
    dimension(c(x0, 10 + short - eps), c(x0, 10), "", off = 0.5)
    text(x0 + 1.08, 10 + short - eps + 0.1, sprintf("still\n%g px\nshort", short - eps),
         adj = c(0, 1), cex = 0.75, col = "grey15")
  }
}
par(op)
```
### Euclidean or Chebyshev distance

The allowance needs a way to measure distance along a segment. The default,
`gap_metric = "euclidean"`, measures ordinary length, so the answer does not
depend on how the drawing is rotated. MLV measures it as the larger of the
horizontal and vertical change (the Chebyshev distance, one raster step), and
`gap_metric = "chebyshev"` reproduces that. Along a diagonal, one Chebyshev
pixel is √2 ≈ 1.41 Euclidean pixels, so a diagonal stem gets a longer reach
than a horizontal or vertical one.

The drawing below has a stem at 45 degrees that stops 1.3 pixels (Euclidean)
short of a horizontal bar. Rotating the drawing by 45 degrees makes the stem
horizontal; the gap is still 1.3 pixels.

```{r metric}
g <- 1.3
diagonal <- mlv_drawing(list(bar = seg(5, 20, 35, 20),
                             stem = seg(20 + g / sqrt(2), 20 - g / sqrt(2), 34, 6)),
                        width = 40, height = 40)
rotated <- rotate_drawing(diagonal, -45)
outcome <- function(d, metric) {
  j <- detect_junctions(d, gap_metric = metric)
  if (nrow(j)) j$type else "none"
}
results <- outer(c(diagonal = "diagonal", rotated = "rotated"),
                 c(euclidean = "euclidean", chebyshev = "chebyshev"),
                 Vectorize(function(r, m) outcome(if (r == "diagonal") diagonal else rotated, m)))
results
```

```{r metric-check, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(results["diagonal", "euclidean"] == "none",
          results["rotated", "euclidean"] == "none",
          results["diagonal", "chebyshev"] == "T",
          results["rotated", "chebyshev"] == "none")
```

Under the Euclidean gap, 1.3 pixels exceeds the 1 pixel allowance in both
orientations, so neither drawing has a junction. Under the Chebyshev gap the
diagonal stem's 1.3 pixel gap is a Chebyshev distance of
1.3 / √2 = `r round(g / sqrt(2), 2)`, within the allowance, so it forms a T;
after rotation the same gap measures 1.3 and is rejected. The junction count
of a drawing measured with the Chebyshev gap can therefore change when the
drawing is rotated.

```{r fig-metric, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = sprintf("A stem stops %g px short of a bar. The blue segment is how far each metric lets the stem's end extend along its own line: %g px everywhere except on the diagonal under the Chebyshev distance, where it reaches %.2f px and meets the bar. Only that extension counts; the dashed outline only shows the metric's shape. Brackets: what is still missing (px).", g, eps, eps * sqrt(2))}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.8, 0.2), oma = c(0, 1.6, 1.4, 0))
for (r in c("diagonal", "rotated")) for (m in c("euclidean", "chebyshev")) {
  d <- compute_contour_properties(if (r == "diagonal") diagonal else rotated, gap_metric = m)
  tip <- d$contours[[2]][1, 1:2]
  far <- d$contours[[2]][1, 3:4]; u <- (tip - far) / sqrt(sum((tip - far)^2))
  # Reach along the stem: the allowance measured in the metric.
  reach <- if (m == "euclidean") eps else eps / max(abs(u))
  meets <- results[r, m] != "none"
  loupe(d, tip + c(-0.5, 0.6), 2.4, property = "junctions", reach = m,
        main = sprintf("reach %.2f px: %s", reach, if (meets) results[r, m] else "no junction"),
        short = sprintf("%.2f px: %s", reach, if (meets) results[r, m] else "none"))
  # The gap, measured along the stem from its end to the bar, and what is left.
  dimension(tip, tip + g * u, sprintf("%g px", g), off = 1.2)
  if (!meets) dimension(tip + reach * u, tip + g * u, sprintf("%.1f", g - reach),
                        off = -0.5, gap = 0.3)
}
mtext(c("Euclidean", "Chebyshev"), side = 3, outer = TRUE, at = c(0.25, 0.75),
      line = 0.2, cex = 0.9)
mtext(c("diagonal stem", "stem on the grid"), side = 2, outer = TRUE, at = c(0.75, 0.25),
      line = 0.3, cex = 0.8, col = "grey25", las = 0)
par(op)
```

The four drawings above are four points of a larger picture. Turning a T
through every angle to the pixel grid, and stopping its stem every 0.05 pixels
short of the bar, shows the whole region in which each metric finds a junction.

```{r decision-map-data}
# A T whose stem stops `gap` px short of a 20 px bar, turned by `angle`
# degrees about the junction. The stem is 15 px long, so the relative limit
# (0.3 of its length) never binds before the 1 px allowance does.
t_at <- function(angle, gap) rotate_drawing(
  mlv_drawing(list(seg(10, 20, 30, 20), seg(20, 20 + gap, 20, 35)), 40, 40), angle, c(20, 20))
angles <- seq(0, 90, by = 2.5); gap_steps <- seq(0, 2, by = 0.05)
found_map <- lapply(c(euclidean = "euclidean", chebyshev = "chebyshev"), function(m)
  outer(angles, gap_steps, Vectorize(function(a, g)
    nrow(detect_junctions(t_at(a, g), gap_metric = m)) > 0)))
sapply(found_map, mean)
```

```{r decision-map-check, include = FALSE}
# Away from the boundary, the detected region is exactly the analytic one.
boundary <- list(euclidean = rep(eps, length(angles)),
                 chebyshev = eps / pmax(abs(cospi(angles / 180)), abs(sinpi(angles / 180))))
for (m in names(found_map)) {
  inside <- outer(boundary[[m]], gap_steps, ">")
  clear <- abs(outer(boundary[[m]], gap_steps, "-")) > 0.03
  stopifnot(identical(found_map[[m]][clear], inside[clear]))
}
```

```{r fig-decision-map, fig.height = 3.3, fig.cap = sprintf("Where a stem stopping short of a bar still forms a junction (shaded), by the stem's angle to the pixel grid and its gap, from detect_junctions() on %d rotated T's per panel. Under the Euclidean distance the allowance is %g px at every angle; under the Chebyshev distance it grows to %.2f px on the diagonal. Points: the figures above (gap in px), filled where a junction is found.", length(found_map[[1]]), eps, eps * sqrt(2))}
cases <- data.frame(angle = c(0, 0, 0, 45), gap = c(near_gap, far_gap, g, g),
                    label = c("0.5", "1.5", "1.3", "1.3"), nudge = c(0, 0.09, -0.09, 0))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.2, 3.4, 1.6, 0.6), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
for (m in names(found_map)) {
  image(angles, gap_steps, found_map[[m]] * 1, col = c("white", "#C6DBEF"),
        xlim = c(-2, 92), ylim = c(0, 2), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", useRaster = TRUE,
        main = if (m == "euclidean") "Euclidean" else "Chebyshev",
        cex.main = 1, font.main = 1)
  lines(angles, boundary[[m]], lwd = 1.4, col = "#0072B2")
  axis(1, at = c(0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90), col = "grey55", col.ticks = "grey55",
       tcl = -0.3, mgp = c(3, 0.5, 0))
  axis(2, at = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2), col = "grey55", col.ticks = "grey55", tcl = -0.3)
  title(xlab = "angle to the pixel grid (°)", line = 2, cex.lab = 0.85)
  if (m == "euclidean") title(ylab = "gap (px)", line = 2.4, cex.lab = 0.85)
  hit <- mapply(function(a, gp) nrow(detect_junctions(t_at(a, gp), gap_metric = m)) > 0,
                cases$angle, cases$gap)
  points(cases$angle, cases$gap, pch = ifelse(hit, 19, 21), bg = "white", cex = 1)
  text(cases$angle, cases$gap + cases$nudge, cases$label, pos = 4, cex = 0.72, offset = 0.4)
  box(col = "grey70", lwd = 0.6)
}
par(op)
```

A methods section can read its tolerance off this map: with the default
Euclidean gap, any stroke that stops within `r eps` pixel of another meets it,
whatever the drawing's orientation; with the Chebyshev gap the tolerance
depends on how the stroke is turned.

## The arm rule

The arms of a junction are the directions in which contours leave the
junction neighbourhood, not the segments that touch it. The definition is
chosen so that three things a viewer ignores do not change the answer: a
stroke that overshoots its target slightly, a stroke that was split into
pieces, and the vertex at which a closed outline happens to start.

```{r arm-cases}
arm_cases <- list(
  overshoot_1 = mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 10, 35, 10), seg(20, 9, 20, 30)), 40, 32),
  overshoot_3 = mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 10, 35, 10), seg(20, 7, 20, 30)), 40, 32),
  split = mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 20, 19.5, 20), seg(19.5, 20, 20.5, 21),
                           seg(20.5, 21, 35, 21)), 40, 32),
  closed = mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 15, 25, 15),
                            polyline(c(15, 15, 35, 25, 15), c(16, 5, 5, 25, 16))), 40, 32))
arm_found <- lapply(arm_cases, detect_junctions)
vapply(arm_found, function(j) if (nrow(j)) j$type else "none", "")
```

```{r arm-check, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(unname(vapply(arm_found, function(j) if (nrow(j)) j$type else "none", "")),
                    c("T", "X", "none", "X")))
```

- **Overshoot.** A stem that crosses the bar by 1 pixel ends inside the 2 pixel
  neighbourhood, so it leaves only downward: three arms, a T. Crossing by 3
  pixels, it leaves upward as well, and the junction is an X.
- **Split polyline.** One near-straight stroke stored as three contours, with
  a short middle piece, touches itself at two points 1.4 pixels apart. They
  merge into one neighbourhood, and only two arms leave it (left and right),
  so there is no junction.
- **Closed contour.** A quadrilateral whose first vertex, (15, 16), lies 1
  pixel below a bar crossing. The outline leaves the neighbourhood twice,
  upward and down to the right, so with the bar's two arms this is an X. The
  start vertex lies inside the neighbourhood, but closed contours are followed
  around their start, so the answer is the same for every start vertex.

```{r closed-starts}
quad <- cbind(c(15, 15, 35, 25), c(16, 5, 5, 25))
start_types <- vapply(1:4, function(k) {
  v <- quad[c(k:4, seq_len(k - 1)), ]
  d <- mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 15, 25, 15), polyline(c(v[, 1], v[1, 1]), c(v[, 2], v[1, 2]))), 40, 32)
  detect_junctions(d)$type
}, "")
start_types
```

```{r fig-arms, fig.height = 4.9, fig.cap = sprintf("The arm rule: a contour adds an arm wherever it leaves the junction neighbourhood (shaded, radius %g px). A 1 px overshoot ends inside the disc (T); a 3 px overshoot adds an arm (X). A stroke stored as three contours has two meeting points whose discs merge into one neighbourhood; the stroke leaves it only twice (grey arrows). A closed outline (inset) starting inside still leaves twice (X).", nbhd)}
centres <- list(overshoot_1 = c(20, 10), overshoot_3 = c(20, 10),
                split = c(20, 20.5), closed = c(15, 15))
titles <- c(overshoot_1 = "1 px overshoot: T", overshoot_3 = "3 px overshoot: X",
            split = "split stroke: no junction", closed = "closed outline: X")
piece_cols <- list(overshoot_1 = "black", overshoot_3 = "black",
                   split = c("black", okabe[["purple"]], okabe[["green"]]),
                   closed = "black")
intersections <- list(overshoot_1 = rbind(c(20, 10)), overshoot_3 = rbind(c(20, 10)),
                      split = rbind(c(19.5, 20), c(20.5, 21)), closed = rbind(c(15, 15)))
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.8, 0.2))
for (name in names(arm_cases)) {
  loupe(arm_cases[[name]], centres[[name]], 5, titles[[name]], grid = FALSE,
        property = "junctions", arms = TRUE, arm_length = 2.8,
        col = piece_cols[[name]])
  p <- intersections[[name]]
  disc(p[, 1], p[, 2], nbhd)
  if (name == "split") exits(p[, 1], p[, 2], c(180, 0), 2.8)
  if (name == "closed") {
    points(15, 16, pch = 4, cex = 1.1, lwd = 2)
    segments(13.9, 17.9, 14.75, 16.3, col = "grey40", lwd = 0.7)
    text(14.1, 18.2, "start vertex", pos = 2, cex = 0.75, offset = 0.2)
    inset(arm_cases$closed, c(10.3, 10.3, 13.6, 13.6), c(10, 10, 20, 20))
  }
}
par(op)
```
A contour that ends inside the neighbourhood contributes no arm in that
direction, and a contour that passes straight through contributes one arm on
each side however many of its vertices lie inside. The arm direction is the
direction of the segment through which the contour leaves, so the angles
between straight arms are exact and do not depend on where the merged
junction position falls.

## Merging nearby crossings

Two crossings within `merge_radius` of each other, including exactly
`merge_radius` apart, are one junction. Merging is
transitive: crossings at 0, 1.8 and 3.6 pixels along a bar merge into one
junction, even though the outer two are 3.6 pixels apart, because each is
within 2 pixels of the middle one.

```{r merge}
two_stems <- function(separation) {
  mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 20, 35, 20), seg(18, 8, 18, 32),
                   seg(18 + separation, 8, 18 + separation, 32)), 40, 40)
}
merged <- detect_junctions(two_stems(1.5))
apart <- detect_junctions(two_stems(2.5))
merged[, c("x", "y", "type", "min_angle")]
merged$arms[[1]]
apart[, c("x", "y", "type", "min_angle")]
chain <- mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 20, 45, 20), seg(18, 8, 18, 32),
                          seg(19.8, 8, 19.8, 32), seg(21.6, 8, 21.6, 32)), 50, 40)
detect_junctions(chain)[, c("x", "type")]
```

```{r merge-check, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(nrow(merged) == 1L, merged$type == "Star", nrow(apart) == 2L,
          all(apart$type == "X"), nrow(detect_junctions(chain)) == 1L)
```

With the stems 1.5 pixels apart, the two crossings merge into one junction at
their midpoint, x = `r merged$x`. It has six arms: the bar's two and both
stems' up and down arms, so it is a Star. The two upward arms point the same
way, so the smallest gap, `min_angle`, is `r merged$min_angle` degrees. At 2.5
pixels apart the crossings stay separate and each is an X. A junction with
gaps of 0 degrees is a sign that nearly parallel contours were merged; if
that is not what the stimulus means, reduce `merge_radius`.

```{r fig-merge, fig.height = 2.9, fig.cap = sprintf("Two stems cross a bar %g px apart (left) and %g px apart (right). Each crossing has a grey disc of radius merge_radius / 2 = %g px, and crossings whose discs touch or overlap merge. On the left they form one six-arm Star, drawn from the merged position between the stems; its upward and downward arms come in coincident pairs (×2). On the right they remain two X-junctions.", 1.5, 2.5, merge_r / 2)}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.8, 0.2))
for (s in c(1.5, 2.5)) {
  d <- two_stems(s); found_s <- detect_junctions(d)
  loupe(d, c(18 + s / 2, 20.8), 4.6, grid = FALSE, property = "junctions",
        arms = TRUE, arm_length = if (nrow(found_s) == 1L) 2.6 else 1.05,
        main = sprintf("%g px apart: %s", s,
                       if (nrow(found_s) == 1L) "one Star" else "two X"))
  disc(c(18, 18 + s), c(20, 20), merge_r / 2)
  dimension(c(18, 24.6), c(18 + s, 24.6), "", off = 1e-9)
  text(18 + s + 0.25, 24.6, sprintf("%g px", s), adj = c(0, 0.5), cex = 0.75, col = "grey15")
}
par(op)
```
## Where `rule = "mlv2023"` differs

`rule = "mlv2023"` reproduces the junction code of the MLV MATLAB toolbox
(commit f12418a), including the behaviours in which the default rule differs,
as recorded in the package's
[differences register](https://github.com/bbuchsbaum/mlvtoolboxR/blob/main/DIFFERENCES.md). Use it only when your numbers must match published MLV
values. Against junctions stored by the original lab's MATLAB runs on 3,017
drawings, it reproduces 395,125 of 395,134 exactly, while the default rule
agrees on 90.1%, every difference being attributed to a recorded MLV difference
or a package definition (qualification results recorded in
[docs/PARITY.md](https://github.com/bbuchsbaum/mlvtoolboxR/blob/main/docs/PARITY.md), not recomputed here). The three drawings below show where the definitions part.

```{r mlv-cases}
mlv_cases <- list(
  diagonal_t = mlv_drawing(list(seg(10, 10, 30, 30), seg(20, 20, 30, 10)), 40, 40),
  vertex_overshoot = mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 10, 35, 10),
                                      polyline(c(20, 20, 20), c(9, 11, 30))), 40, 32),
  closed_start = arm_cases$closed)
compare <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mlv_cases), function(name) {
  e <- detect_junctions(mlv_cases[[name]])
  m <- detect_junctions(mlv_cases[[name]], rule = "mlv2023")
  data.frame(case = name, exit_type = e$type, exit_min = round(e$min_angle, 1),
             mlv_type = m$type, mlv_min = round(m$min_angle, 1))
}))
compare
```

```{r mlv-check, include = FALSE}
mlv_arms_t <- detect_junctions(mlv_cases$diagonal_t, rule = "mlv2023")$arms[[1]]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(mlv_arms_t, c(45, 45, 225))))
stopifnot(identical(compare$exit_type, c("T", "T", "X")),
          identical(compare$mlv_type, c("T", "X", "T")),
          compare$mlv_min[1] == 0, compare$exit_min[1] == 90)
# One drawing under both rules, side by side: arms (orange), the smallest gap
# (the reported min angle), the neighbourhood disc, and in the published
# panel the default arms as grey ghosts.
compare_rules <- function(name, centre, marks = function() NULL) {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 2.6, 0.2), cex = 0.9)
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (rule in c("exit", "mlv2023")) {
    d <- compute_contour_properties(mlv_cases[[name]], rule = rule)
    j <- d$junctions
    plot(d, property = "junctions", arms = TRUE, gaps = "min", arm_length = 3.6,
         lwd = 2, axes = FALSE, frame = FALSE,
         xlim = centre[1] + c(-6.5, 6.5), ylim = centre[2] + c(4.6, -4.6),
         reference_junctions = if (rule == "mlv2023") detect_junctions(mlv_cases[[name]]))
    title(main = sprintf("%s\n%s, min angle %g°",
                         if (rule == "exit") "default" else "published (mlv2023)",
                         j$type, round(j$min_angle)), cex.main = 1, font.main = 1)
    disc(j$x, j$y, nbhd)
    marks()
  }
}
```

**Diagonal T (MLV-M007).** A bar from (10, 10) to (30, 30) with a stem from
its midpoint up and to the right. The stem is perpendicular to the bar, so
the gaps are 90, 90 and 180 degrees and `min_angle` is
`r compare$exit_min[1]`. MLV measures arms that pass through the junction
with y pointing up but arms that end there with y pointing down. The bar's
arms, at 135 and 315 degrees, are mirrored to
`r paste(round(setdiff(round(mlv_arms_t, 6), 45)), collapse = " and ")` and
45 degrees, so one of them coincides with the stem and `min_angle` is
`r compare$mlv_min[1]`. The type is still T, so the difference shows only
when angles are analysed.

```{r fig-mlv, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = sprintf("The diagonal T under the default rule (left) and the published rule (right). Orange: the arms each rule assigns; grey open arrowheads: the default arms, for comparison; shaded disc: the junction neighbourhood (radius %g px). The published rule mirrors the bar's arms, so one lies on the stem (×2, min angle 0°) and the other on no ink.", nbhd)}
compare_rules("diagonal_t", c(20, 20))
```

**Overshoot with a vertex inside the neighbourhood (MLV-M024).** The stem
overshoots the bar by 1 pixel, as before, but is drawn as two segments with
a vertex at y = 11. MLV makes every segment of a contour inside the
neighbourhood an arm, so both stem segments count and the T becomes an X
with a 0 degree gap. The default rule follows the contour out of the
neighbourhood and finds one downward arm.

```{r fig-mlv-overshoot, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "The overshooting stem drawn as two segments, with a vertex (open circle) inside the neighbourhood. The default rule follows the stem out of the neighbourhood and finds one downward arm (T). The published rule gives each of the stem's two segments an arm; the two coincide (×2, min angle 0°), and it reports an X."}
compare_rules("vertex_overshoot", c(20, 11.4),
              function() points(20, 11, pch = 21, bg = "white", cex = 1.1, lwd = 1.3))
```

**Closed contour starting inside the neighbourhood (MLV-M026).** MLV treats
a closed contour as ending at its first vertex. Starting at (15, 16), the
outline appears to end inside the neighbourhood, so it contributes one arm
rather than two and MLV reports a T; started at any other vertex it reports
an X. The default rule reports X for every start vertex.

```{r mlv-starts}
vapply(1:4, function(k) {
  v <- quad[c(k:4, seq_len(k - 1)), ]
  d <- mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 15, 25, 15), polyline(c(v[, 1], v[1, 1]), c(v[, 2], v[1, 2]))), 40, 32)
  detect_junctions(d, rule = "mlv2023")$type
}, "")
```

```{r fig-mlv-closed, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = sprintf("The closed outline of the arm-rule figure, which starts inside the neighbourhood (cross: its start vertex). The default rule follows the outline round its start and finds two arms, up and down to the right, so with the bar's two it reports an X (min angle %g°). The published rule treats the outline as ending at its start, assigns it one arm and reports a T.", compare$exit_min[3])}
compare_rules("closed_start", c(15, 15.2),
              function() points(15, 16, pch = 4, cex = 1.1, lwd = 2))
```

Under `rule = "mlv2023"` the `arms` column holds the directions MLV assigns,
in MLV's own conventions, which is why the figures above can show them. The same
rule also turns the split stroke of the previous section into a T
(`r detect_junctions(arm_cases$split, rule = "mlv2023")$type`), because its
short middle piece is attached by its start point. `rule = "mlv2023"` always
uses the Chebyshev gap.

## What junction statistics measure

Junction features enter analyses in three forms, all computed from the table
above.

- **Type counts.** `contour_statistics(x, "junction_type")` counts junctions
  of each type, T, Y, X, Arrow and Star, in that order.
- **Angle distribution.** `contour_statistics(x, "junction_angle")` is a
  histogram of each junction's smallest gap, `min_angle`, over 0 to 120
  degrees (no junction can have a smallest gap above 120, since at least
  three gaps sum to 360).
- **Density.** `average_property(x, "junctions")` is the number of junctions
  per 10,000 pixels of contour length, and `normalize = TRUE` expresses the
  histograms in the same units. Junction counts grow with the amount of ink,
  so density is usually the quantity to compare between drawings.

Per contour (`by = "contour"`, and in `feature_table()`), each junction is
counted once for every contour that takes part in it. To see these numbers on
known input, place the six gallery drawings side by side on one canvas:

```{r statistics}
shift <- function(z, dx, dy) { z[, c(1, 3)] <- z[, c(1, 3)] + dx; z[, c(2, 4)] <- z[, c(2, 4)] + dy; z }
offsets <- expand.grid(dx = c(0, 40, 80), dy = c(0, 40))
cells <- lapply(seq_along(gallery), function(k)
  lapply(gallery[[k]]$contours, shift, offsets$dx[k], offsets$dy[k]))
sheet <- mlv_drawing(unlist(cells, recursive = FALSE), width = 120, height = 80)
types <- contour_statistics(sheet, properties = "junction_type")
types[, c("label", "value", "units")]
angles <- contour_statistics(sheet, properties = "junction_angle")
angles[, c("lower", "upper", "value")]
average_property(sheet, "junctions")
```

```{r statistics-check, include = FALSE}
total_length <- sum(as.data.frame(sheet)$length)
angles5 <- contour_statistics(sheet, properties = "junction_angle", bins = 5)
stopifnot(identical(angles5$value, c(0, 0, 2, 2, 1)),
          identical(angles$value, c(0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 2, 1)))
gaps <- vapply(found[c("Y", "Arrow", "Star")], function(j) j$min_angle[1], 0)
stopifnot(all(abs(gaps - c(120, 60, 60)) < 1e-12))
stopifnot(all(types$value == 1),
          isTRUE(all.equal(average_property(sheet, "junctions"), 5 / total_length * 1e4)))
```

The sheet holds one junction of each type; the L contributes none. The
density is 5 junctions over `r round(total_length, 1)` pixels of contour,
`r round(average_property(sheet, "junctions"), 1)` per 10,000 pixels.

With the default 8 bins the angle histogram's edges fall every 15 degrees,
exactly at 60, 90 and 120 degrees, the smallest gaps of the commonest
junctions. A gap that falls on an edge enters the upper bin. A gap computed
from trigonometry can come out a rounding error either side of the exact
angle; on the computer that built this page the smallest gaps of the Y, Arrow
and Star above are `r paste(sprintf("%.17g", gaps), collapse = ", ")`
degrees. Every histogram therefore treats a
value within 1e-9 × max(1, |edge|) of a bin edge as lying on the edge, so
mathematically equal gaps share a bin on every platform: here the Arrow and
Star (60) share the bin from 60 to 75 degrees, the T and X (90) the bin from
90 to 105, and the Y (120) the last bin. The tolerance is far above rounding
residue and far below any difference between real gaps. A bin count whose
edges avoid the expected angles, such as 5 (edges at 0, 24, 48, 72, 96 and
120 degrees), keeps the bins away from the edges altogether:

```{r angle-bins}
contour_statistics(sheet, properties = "junction_angle", bins = 5)[, c("lower", "upper", "value")]
```

## Choosing settings

- Keep the defaults (`rule = "exit"`, Euclidean gap, 1 pixel allowance, 2
  pixel merge and neighbourhood radii) for new work. They do not depend on
  contour direction, numbering, closed-contour start vertex or rotation.
- Scale `absolute_epsilon`, `merge_radius` and `endpoint_radius` with the
  stroke width and resolution of your stimuli. In a feature specification
  (`feature_spec(junction = list(...))`) they are stated in the
  specification's spatial units and converted for each drawing.
- Use `rule = "mlv2023"` only to reproduce published MLV values.
